hook: Buffie The Body reveals she was in her *40s*
dek: Her Tamron Hall interview reignites hip hop's debate over the women who defined it.

slides.label: What happened
slides.text: Buffie 'The Body' Lewis sat down with *The Tamron Hall Show* on Oct. 9 to revisit her video vixen days.

slides.label: The reveal
slides.text: She says she was already in her *40s* while many women working beside her were in their 20s.

slides.label: The bigger moment
slides.text: Her interview lands the same week *The Joe Budden Podcast* revisited the video vixen era on Oct. 7.

slides.label: Pushback
slides.text: Former vixen Gloria Velez clapped back: *'Maybe it's why are y'all so obsessed with us?'*

slides.label: How it started
slides.text: Swimsuit photos of Lewis leaked online without her permission, leading to a King magazine feature.

slides.label: Her rise
slides.text: That buzz fueled her role in *50 Cent and Tony Yayo's 'So Seductive'* video in 2005, plus a part as Big Booty Judy in *'ATL'* (2006).

slides.label: Life now
slides.text: Today Lewis runs her *Bodynomics* fitness platform and *Brick Built* apparel brand, sharing workouts and home projects.

slides.label: Why it matters
slides.text: It shows how Black women who built hip hop's visual culture are now shaping fitness, fashion and media on their own terms.

caption_instagram:
Buffie 'The Body' Lewis just revealed on The Tamron Hall Show that she was already in her 40s while many of the women working alongside her in hip hop's video vixen era were in their 20s. The reveal comes as hip hop revisits the women who defined 2000s music videos, with The Joe Budden Podcast sparking the conversation and former vixen Gloria Velez clapping back at the idea that these women disappeared.

Lewis became a household name after appearing in 50 Cent and Tony Yayo's 'So Seductive' video in 2005, later landing magazine covers and a role in 'ATL.' Two decades later she runs Bodynomics and Brick Built, trading photoshoots for workouts, gardening and carpentry.

Her story is proof that the women who shaped hip hop's visual culture built real lives and businesses long after the cameras moved on, per The Grio.

Buffie 'The Body' Lewis built a public identity in hip hop's video vixen era of the 2000s, then quietly built something more lasting: two businesses.

Her recent appearance on The Tamron Hall Show revealed she was already in her 40s while many women working beside her were in their 20s, a detail that reframes how we think about longevity in entertainment. Her interview lands as hip hop revisits that era more broadly, with The Joe Budden Podcast prompting former vixen Gloria Velez to push back on the narrative that these women vanished.

Lewis went from an unplanned leak of swimsuit photos to appearing in 50 Cent and Tony Yayo's 'So Seductive' video, magazine covers and a role in 'ATL.' Two decades later she runs Bodynomics, a fitness platform, and Brick Built, an apparel brand, per The Grio.

For founders building a personal brand, her path is a case study in controlling the narrative after the spotlight moves on. Will the next generation of creators manage that transition any differently? Yes or no?
